passages.title: The Last Crossing
passages.topic: a ferry pilot and his granddaughter before a bridge opens
passages.text:
By the last week of June, the ferry had become a sort of museum piece that still happened to float. Nell Okafor stood at the rail of the Heron, scraping gull droppings from the brass with a putty knife, and listened to her grandfather argue with the engine in a low, affectionate growl.

“Four more days,” she said. “Then the bridge opens, and nobody will ever need us again.”

“Nobody needed us before the bridge, either,” Grandpa Walt said, not looking up. “They just wanted us. It’s a different thing, and a better one.”

Nell did not see the difference. All week she had watched commuters cross the river for the last time, nodding at the Heron as though it were a retiring teacher. A man in a gray suit had even shaken Walt’s hand and said, “End of an era.” Walt had only smiled and offered him coffee.

That evening, while Walt counted the cash box, Nell found a wooden crate beneath the pilot’s bench. Inside, wrapped in oilcloth, lay stacks of small brass plates, each stamped with a name and a year. She lifted one and read, “Ines Doyle, first crossing, age six.”

“I started those the week I took the job,” Walt said from the doorway. “Every child’s first ride. I kept meaning to put them up somewhere.”

“There must be hundreds.”

“Nine hundred and some.” He took the plate and rubbed it against his sleeve. “Folks think a ferry carries people across water. Mostly it carries them across their own ordinary days. A boy going to his first job, a woman going to the hospital. I’m not sad the bridge is coming, Nellie. A bridge will be quicker. I’m only sad that nobody will pause.”

Nell thought of the man in the gray suit, who had crossed without once looking at the river. Something in her chest shifted.

On the final morning she arrived early, before the sun had burned the mist off the water, carrying a borrowed drill. By the time the first passengers climbed aboard, rows of brass plates gleamed along the cabin wall, with one space left empty in the top corner.

“What’s that blank spot for?” asked a small boy clutching his mother’s hand.

“For you,” said Nell, and held out the stamp.

passages.title: The Cracked Bowl
passages.topic: a student potter learns from a flawed piece
passages.text:
The bowl sat on the judging table, and everyone in the art room pretended not to look at it. A hairline crack ran from the rim to the base, thin as a spider’s thread, and Dev Malhotra could not stop staring at it.

Three weeks earlier, Dev had been so sure of himself that he had turned down Ms. Carver’s offer of extra help. “I’ve thrown forty of these,” he had said, shrugging. The clay had felt familiar under his hands, the wheel humming like an old refrigerator. Eager to finish, he had set the bowl beside the heater so it would be ready for the kiln by Friday. He told himself the bowl did not mind.

His friend Priya had noticed. “Isn’t that too close to the heat?” she asked. “Clay dries from the outside in, you know. Ms. Carver said—”

“Ms. Carver says a lot,” Dev answered. He was not proud of how it sounded, even then.

Now the judge, a potter from town with clay permanently ground into her knuckles, lifted the bowl and turned it slowly in the light. Dev’s stomach folded in on itself. He waited for the verdict the way one waits for a wave.

“Whose is this?” she asked.

He raised his hand, half expecting the room to laugh.

“The glaze is lovely,” she said. “The shape is confident. And the crack,” she ran a thumbnail beside it, “is the most honest thing in this room. It tells me exactly what happened, and when.” She set the bowl down gently. “Every potter I know has a bowl like this one. The difference is whether it teaches them anything.”

No ribbon came his way that day. But afterward, while the others crowded around the cookie table, Dev walked to Ms. Carver’s desk. “Would your offer of extra help still stand?” he asked.

“Bring a lump of clay,” she said, “and your patience. Both run short on Fridays.”

Priya, passing with a paper cup, bumped his elbow and grinned. “About time.”

passages.title: Case File: The Tomato Thief
passages.topic: a young detective misreads a quiet neighbor
passages.text:
I had been keeping a notebook on Mr. Lindqvist since the first week of August. Case file, I called it, in my best block letters. Entry one: Moves into 14B. Never waves. Entry four: Carries a watering can out at dawn, when nobody is watching. Entry six: Comes back with his coat pockets bulging.

It was obvious to me what was happening. The community garden behind our building had been losing tomatoes all summer, and the one person who never waved was the only one awake before the sun. My friend Zoe wasn’t convinced. “Maybe he just likes tomatoes,” she said, which is exactly the kind of thing a bad detective says.

On the first Saturday of September, I set my alarm for 5:15 and crept down the back stairs in my socks. Mist hung over the plots like breath on a window. Mr. Lindqvist was already there, kneeling beside the sunflowers, and I crouched behind the compost bin with my notebook open and my heart pounding like a drum solo.

He filled his watering can. He pressed a finger into the soil, frowned, and gave the thirsty beans a second pass. Then he pulled a folded plastic bag from his coat and began to pick, not tomatoes, but weeds and the soft, split fruit the squirrels had already ruined. Into the bag they went.

“Ah,” he said suddenly, without turning around. “Your notebook is rather bright. Orange, is it?”

My face went hot as a skillet. “I wasn’t—”

“Detective work. Good. It takes patience.” He stood, his knees cracking. “Mrs. Alvarez’s plot goes untended now that her hip keeps her indoors, so I promised to water it before work. I do not wave because, to be frank, I am shy, and English gives me trouble before breakfast.”

I looked at his pockets, where the lumpy bag sat. Then I looked at my notebook. Entry seven stayed unwritten for a very long time.

“Would it help,” I finally said, “if I carried a second bucket for the beans?”

He smiled, an actual, visible smile. “It would be an enormous help.”

The tomato thief, by the way, turned out to be a family of raccoons. But that is another case file.

passages.title: Moving Day
passages.topic: a speaker's last night in a childhood home
passages.text:
The house is a shell I have outgrown,
and the rooms still hum, faintly, with the sea
of my own voice, the way a shell will always keep
a distant ocean long after the tide is gone.
In the hallway the boxes lean together
like tired gulls waiting for some signal to lift and fly.

Pencil lines climb the kitchen doorframe, crooked and faded,
each small, penciled notch a year I stood against the wood
and stretched my spine on tiptoe, as if I could argue
with the ceiling and finally win.
My father’s handwriting labels every line,
the dates crowded and slanting, proud as small bright flags.

Tonight my own footsteps echo back too quickly,
thin and bare against the stripped-down, echoing walls.
The pale squares where the photographs once hung
look startled to be shown so plain, so naked
to the light. I almost want to apologize out loud
to the empty rooms for taking all the noise.

I run my palm along the banister,
worn smooth by years of hurrying, hopeful hands,
and understand that leaving is a kind
of carrying: not the chairs or the lamps or the heavy boxes
but what they witnessed. When the door clicks shut,
I will carry, in some quiet room of me, the height of every year I grew here.

passages.title: The Waggle Dance
passages.text:
When a honeybee returns to the hive after finding a rich patch of flowers, she does not simply announce her good luck. Inside the dark, crowded hive, she performs a precise routine that scientists call the waggle dance, and her sisters read it like a set of directions.

The dance follows a simple pattern. The bee walks forward in a straight line while shaking her body rapidly from side to side, then circles back to her starting point and repeats the line, alternating loops to the left and the right. The straight, shaking stretch is the part that carries the message.

The angle of that stretch reveals direction. Because the dance takes place on the vertical wall of the honeycomb, the bees use straight up as a stand-in for the position of the sun. If the bee waggles straight up, the food lies in the direction of the sun. If she waggles thirty degrees to the right of vertical, the flowers lie thirty degrees to the right of the sun.

The length of the waggle reveals distance. The longer the bee shakes along the line, the farther away the flowers lie, while a quick, short waggle points to a patch just outside the hive. Observers have also noticed that bees repeat the dance more times, and with more energy, when the food is especially rich. The dance therefore tells nestmates not only where to go but also whether the trip is worth the effort.

Remarkably, the system adjusts as the day passes. Because the sun moves across the sky, the dancers gradually change their angle so that newcomers do not fly off in the wrong direction. Even in total darkness, the watching bees crowd close and follow the performance by touch and vibration.

The waggle dance shows that communication does not require words. With nothing more than movement, a tiny insect can store, compress, and share information about a place she has seen, and a whole colony benefits from her report.

passages.title: Sounding the Deep
passages.topic: how people learned to measure the ocean floor
passages.text:
For most of human history, the ocean floor was as hidden as the far side of the moon. Sailors knew where land ended and water began, but what lay beneath their hulls was largely guesswork.

The earliest method for measuring depth was simple and slow. A sailor tied a lead weight to a long rope, dropped it overboard, and counted how much line ran out before the weight touched bottom. Crews called this process sounding. It worked well enough in harbors, yet in deep water the rope could drift with currents or run out of length, and a single measurement could take hours.

Everything changed when engineers learned to use sound itself. An echo sounder sends a short pulse of sound from a ship’s hull straight down. The pulse travels through the water, strikes the seafloor, and bounces back. Because the speed of sound in water is known, a device can multiply that speed by the time the echo takes to return, then divide by two, since the sound traveled down and back. The result is the depth, calculated in a fraction of a second.

Modern ships have improved the idea. Instead of a single narrow beam, multibeam systems send out a fan of pulses that sweep a wide strip of the seafloor at once. As the ship moves forward, the strips link together into detailed maps showing mountains, canyons, and long ridges beneath the waves.

These maps are far more than curiosities. Engineers use them to plan routes for underwater cables, and ship captains rely on them to avoid hazards. Scientists use them to study how currents flow around underwater mountains and where ocean life gathers.

It may seem that satellites have already settled the matter, but they can only suggest broad shapes by measuring tiny bumps on the sea’s surface. A ship’s sonar still provides far sharper detail, and because a ship can chart only the strip it passes over, mapping the vast ocean continues one patient sweep at a time.

passages.title: Roofs That Grow
passages.topic: how green roofs work and what they cost
passages.text:
Look down from a tall building in almost any large city and you will see a landscape of tar, gravel, and metal. Roofs make up a large share of urban surfaces, and most of them sit empty. A growing number of builders see that space as an opportunity, and they are covering it with plants.

A green roof is built in layers. On top of the waterproof membrane lies a barrier that keeps roots from damaging the building, then a drainage layer, then a lightweight soil mix, and finally the plants. Designers often choose hardy species such as sedum, a low, fleshy plant that tolerates drought and wind.

The benefits begin with water. When heavy rain strikes an ordinary roof, it runs quickly into gutters and storm drains, which can overflow in a big storm. A green roof soaks up much of that water, releasing it slowly or letting plants return it to the air. The roof therefore acts like a sponge, easing the strain on the drains below.

Temperature is a second advantage. Dark roofs absorb sunlight and warm the air around them, which is one reason city centers often run hotter than the surrounding countryside. Plants and soil, in contrast, cool themselves by releasing moisture and shading the surface beneath. Inside the building, the extra layers also insulate, so less energy is needed for heating in winter and cooling in summer.

Green roofs are not without drawbacks. Wet soil is heavy, so many older buildings cannot support one without reinforcement. Installation costs more than a conventional roof, and plants need some care, especially during their first year. Supporters respond that savings on energy and repairs can offset these costs over time, though results vary from building to building.

Even so, the idea keeps spreading. For a city, a green roof is a small patch of countryside in the sky: part sponge, part blanket, and part garden.

passages.title: Keep the Library Open
passages.topic: an argument for an after-school library hour
passages.text:
Every afternoon at 3:15, the doors of Eastgate Middle School’s library swing shut and the lights go off. I believe that decision is a mistake. Our school should keep the library open for one hour after the final bell, because doing so would help students finish their work and reach books they cannot get anywhere else.

First, consider homework. At home, many students share a single computer with siblings or have no quiet place to spread out their papers. In a survey conducted by the student council last spring, 140 of the 200 eighth graders who responded said they struggle to find a quiet place to study. An open library would give those students a table, a printer, and a working internet connection at no cost.

Second, an extra hour would strengthen our reading culture. When the Millbrook public library, a few blocks from our school, extended its weekday hours last year, its librarian reported that far more teenagers began checking out books. Students who can browse the shelves in the afternoon are more likely to pick up a book they would otherwise never have found.

Some people argue that the plan would cost too much because a staff member would have to stay late. This concern is fair, but the expense should be small. Parent volunteers have already offered to supervise two afternoons a week, and the principal could assign a teacher on the remaining days.

Also, the library has a beautiful blue carpet that was installed three years ago, and blue happens to be my favorite color. Students deserve to enjoy such a lovely space for as long as possible.

Finally, my cousin attends a school in another state that closed its library at the end of last year, and her grades fell from straight A’s to mostly B’s. Clearly, closing a library hurts students’ grades.

In short, an open library costs little and helps many. The school board should approve the plan before next semester.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that Walt values the ferry’s place in people’s lives more than its practical use?
items.answer: “Mostly it carries them across their own ordinary days.”

wrong.text: “A bridge will be quicker.”
wrong.why: Picks a true statement that is about speed, not about what the ferry means to people.

wrong.text: “Nell found a wooden crate beneath the pilot’s bench.”
wrong.why: Chooses a plot detail that sets up the discovery but shows nothing about Walt’s values.

wrong.text: “A man in a gray suit had even shaken Walt’s hand and said, ‘End of an era.’”
wrong.why: Confuses another character’s respect for the ferry with Walt’s own view.

items.explanation: Walt says the ferry carries people through their “ordinary days,” which shows he values its role in their lives, not just its use as transportation.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the passage?
items.answer: Everyday routines gain meaning from the human moments they hold, and those moments deserve attention.

wrong.text: Progress always replaces the old ways, so people should accept change quickly and stop dwelling on the past.
wrong.why: Over-generalizes; Walt accepts the bridge but the story is about noticing, not hurrying.

wrong.text: Young people should help older relatives finish their life’s work.
wrong.why: Too narrow; focuses on Nell’s help rather than the idea the story develops.

wrong.text: Old boats are more dependable than modern bridges are.
wrong.why: Reverses the story, where Walt admits the bridge will be quicker.

items.explanation: Walt’s comments about “ordinary days” and people who “pause,” along with Nell’s display of the plates, develop the idea that everyday moments matter.

items.prompt: How does Nell’s discovery of the crate of brass plates affect the story?
items.answer: She comes to understand what the ferry means to her grandfather and decides to honor it.

wrong.text: She becomes angry that her grandfather kept such a large secret hidden from her for so many years.
wrong.why: Assumes the discovery causes conflict; Nell never shows anger.

wrong.text: She decides that the opening of the bridge should be delayed.
wrong.why: Confuses honoring the ferry with stopping the bridge; she never tries to stop it.

wrong.text: She learns that the ferry earned more money than she believed.
wrong.why: Focuses on the cash box mentioned nearby, not the meaning of the plates.

items.explanation: After the plates and Walt’s explanation, Nell’s “chest shifted,” and the next morning she mounts the plates, showing a change in understanding.

items.prompt: In the first paragraph, what does the phrase “a sort of museum piece” suggest about the ferry?
items.answer: It is treated as a relic of the past rather than something people still need.

wrong.text: It is fragile and must be handled with great care.
wrong.why: Takes “museum” literally as a place for delicate objects.

wrong.text: It is valuable enough that collectors from across the region would want to buy it.
wrong.why: Reads “museum piece” as high monetary value.

wrong.text: It is crowded each day with visitors who come to tour it.
wrong.why: Assumes the ferry has become a tourist attraction, which the passage never says.

items.explanation: The phrase, followed by “still happened to float,” suggests the ferry is now seen as an old object kept around mostly for the past.

items.prompt: Early in the passage Walt says, “They just wanted us,” and the narrator states that Nell “did not see the difference.” What effect does this create for readers?
items.answer: Readers sense Walt’s hidden point before Nell does, which builds anticipation for her change.

wrong.text: Readers begin to distrust Walt’s account of what the ferry means.
wrong.why: Reverses the effect; the narrator invites trust in Walt’s wisdom.

wrong.text: Readers find humor in how foolishly Nell is behaving toward her grandfather throughout the scene.
wrong.why: Mistakes a gentle misunderstanding for a comic mistake; the tone is thoughtful.

wrong.text: Readers are left unsure whether the ferry will really stop running.
wrong.why: Confuses the main conflict; the bridge’s opening is stated as certain.

items.explanation: The narrator tells readers that Nell misses the difference Walt describes, so readers see his point early and wait for her to catch up.

items.prompt: Which detail from the passage best supports the inference that Dev’s actions caused the crack in the bowl?
items.answer: He set the bowl beside the heater so it would be ready by Friday.

wrong.text: He had already thrown forty bowls before this one and felt sure of himself.
wrong.why: True and shows confidence, but it does not explain how the crack formed.

wrong.text: The wheel hummed like an old refrigerator.
wrong.why: A descriptive detail unrelated to the cause of the crack.

wrong.text: The judge was a potter with clay ground into her knuckles.
wrong.why: Uses a detail about the judge, who only examines the result.

items.explanation: Priya warns that clay “dries from the outside in,” and Dev still dries the bowl by the heater, which connects his rushing to the crack.

items.prompt: How does the judge’s speech about the crack affect Dev’s decision at the end?
items.answer: It leads him to ask for the extra help he had earlier refused.

wrong.text: It persuades him to enter a different contest.
wrong.why: Invents an outcome; the passage shows no new contest.

wrong.text: It causes him to argue with Priya about her warning.
wrong.why: Reverses the ending, where Priya grins and supports him.

wrong.text: It convinces him that the judge was wrong to praise the glaze.
wrong.why: Misreads the judge’s praise as an insult.

items.explanation: After hearing that a flawed bowl teaches something, Dev walks to Ms. Carver’s desk and asks whether her offer still stands.

items.prompt: The passage opens at the judging table and then moves back three weeks. How does this structure contribute to the story?
items.answer: It shows the result first, so readers wonder how the crack happened and read on for the cause.

wrong.text: It hides Dev’s mistakes until the very end of the story so that the final scene feels like a surprise.
wrong.why: Dev’s mistakes appear in the flashback, well before the ending.

wrong.text: It shows that the story is mostly about Priya’s memories.
wrong.why: Priya appears, but the point of view stays with Dev.

wrong.text: It slows the plot so that the judge seems less important.
wrong.why: The judge’s scene is the story’s turning point, not minimized by the flashback.

items.explanation: Beginning with the crack creates curiosity, and the flashback then answers how it happened before returning to the judging.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of this story about Dev?
items.answer: Owning a mistake and learning from it matters more than the failure itself.

wrong.text: Talent is enough for success when a person practices carefully and works alone.
wrong.why: Contradicts the story, where Dev’s confidence leads to failure.

wrong.text: Friends should avoid pointing out one another’s mistakes.
wrong.why: Reverses Priya’s role; her warning was correct.

wrong.text: Judges should reward effort even when a piece is flawed.
wrong.why: Shifts to a rule for judges; the story is about Dev’s growth.

items.explanation: The judge says the difference is “whether it teaches them anything,” and Dev responds by asking for help, developing the theme of learning from error.

items.prompt: The narrator says Dev “waited for the verdict the way one waits for a wave.” What does this simile suggest?
items.answer: He felt tense and unable to stop what was about to happen.

wrong.text: He felt calm and relaxed, as if at a beach.
wrong.why: Takes the water image literally and ignores his stomach “folding in.”

wrong.text: He felt excited and hoped the judge would react in a dramatic way.
wrong.why: Confuses anticipation with eager hope; Dev is dreading the verdict.

wrong.text: He felt confused about what the judge meant to say.
wrong.why: The judge has not yet spoken, so Dev cannot be confused by her words.

items.explanation: A wave cannot be stopped, so the comparison, paired with his “stomach folded in on itself,” shows dread and helplessness.

items.prompt: Which detail the narrator observes in the garden best shows that her suspicion of Mr. Lindqvist was mistaken?
items.answer: He picks weeds and fruit already ruined by squirrels, not healthy tomatoes.

wrong.text: He is already in the garden when she arrives, long before the sun has fully risen.
wrong.why: Fits her suspicion as much as it fits his innocence.

wrong.text: He notices her hiding behind the compost bin.
wrong.why: Shows he is observant but not what he is doing in the garden.

wrong.text: He kneels beside the sunflowers at sunrise.
wrong.why: Describes where he is without showing what he is doing.

items.explanation: Picking weeds and spoiled fruit shows he is cleaning the garden, not stealing from it.

items.prompt: Which idea is most strongly developed by the narrator’s experience in the garden?
items.answer: Judging people by partial evidence can lead to unfair conclusions.

wrong.text: Quiet people are usually hiding something.
wrong.why: Reverses the story, in which the quiet man is shown to be kind.

wrong.text: Keeping detailed records is the best way to learn the truth about other people.
wrong.why: The notebook leads the narrator astray, so it is not the lesson.

wrong.text: Neighbors should spend more time working in the garden.
wrong.why: A detail of the setting, not the idea the plot develops.

items.explanation: The narrator’s notes make Mr. Lindqvist look guilty, but his explanation reveals he was helping, so the story shows how partial evidence misleads.

items.prompt: What does Mr. Lindqvist’s explanation in the garden reveal about his character?
items.answer: He is shy and responsible, and he keeps a promise to help a neighbor.

wrong.text: He is angry about being watched and wants to scare the narrator into leaving.
wrong.why: His tone is polite and even encouraging.

wrong.text: He is boastful and wants credit for caring for the garden.
wrong.why: He never seeks praise and shares the story only when questioned.

wrong.text: He is confused about how the community garden is run.
wrong.why: He knows which plot belongs to whom and why it needs water.

items.explanation: He says he promised to water Mrs. Alvarez’s plot and admits to being shy, which shows both his responsibility and his reason for not waving.

items.prompt: The narrator thinks Mr. Lindqvist is the thief, but readers can see signs that he is helping. What effect does this difference create?
items.answer: It creates gentle humor, since readers recognize the narrator’s mistake before she does.

wrong.text: It builds suspense about whether Mr. Lindqvist is really guilty of stealing the tomatoes all summer.
wrong.why: The clues point away from guilt, so suspense is limited.

wrong.text: It makes readers distrust the narrator’s honesty in general.
wrong.why: She is mistaken, not dishonest.

wrong.text: It makes readers feel sorry for the raccoons in the garden.
wrong.why: The raccoons appear only in the last line.

items.explanation: Her detail-by-detail suspicion, such as the watering can and bulging pockets, is funny because readers can read those clues as signs of care.

items.prompt: The passage opens with the narrator’s notebook entries and ends with “Entry seven stayed unwritten for a very long time.” How does this structure add to the story’s meaning?
items.answer: The early entries show her suspicion, and the blank entry shows that her view has changed.

wrong.text: The entries prove that her suspicions about Mr. Lindqvist were correct from the very beginning.
wrong.why: Reverses the plot, since the entries rest on misread clues.

wrong.text: The blank entry shows that she has given up being a detective.
wrong.why: She still jokes about “another case file,” so she has not quit.

wrong.text: The entries show Zoe is the main detective in the story.
wrong.why: Zoe is only a minor character who questions the case.

items.explanation: The numbered entries set up her theory, and the long pause over entry seven shows she no longer trusts that theory.

items.prompt: Which lines from the poem best support the idea that the house holds a record of the speaker’s growth?
items.answer: “each small notch a year I stood against the wood / and stretched my spine”

wrong.text: “the boxes lean together / like tired gulls”
wrong.why: Describes the packing, not the speaker’s growth.

wrong.text: “The pale squares where the photographs once hung / look startled to be shown so plain”
wrong.why: Shows what is missing from the walls rather than growth over time.

wrong.text: “worn smooth by years of hurrying hands”
wrong.why: Refers to many people’s use of the banister, not the speaker’s growth.

items.explanation: The pencil notches on the doorframe mark each year the speaker grew taller.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the poem?
items.answer: Leaving a place is hard, but the meaning of lived experience goes with us.

wrong.text: Moving is easier when a family labels and packs its belongings carefully ahead of time.
wrong.why: Picks up on the boxes and labels but ignores the poem’s deeper reflection.

wrong.text: A house keeps its memories only while its photographs stay on the walls.
wrong.why: Reverses the ending, in which memories remain after the photographs are gone.

wrong.text: Growing up means learning to argue with those in charge.
wrong.why: Over-reads the line about arguing with the ceiling, which is about growing taller.

items.explanation: The speaker says “leaving is a kind of carrying” and will keep the “height of every year,” so memories travel with the person.

items.prompt: In the fourth stanza, the speaker runs a palm along the banister. What does this action lead to?
items.answer: It prompts the speaker to realize that memories can be carried away.

wrong.text: It makes the speaker regret the decision to move away from the old house.
wrong.why: The speaker feels loss but never expresses regret.

wrong.text: It makes the speaker decide to ask the family to stay.
wrong.why: No such decision appears; the speaker accepts the move.

wrong.text: It reminds the speaker of an argument with a parent.
wrong.why: The only parent mentioned is remembered with fondness.

items.explanation: Right after touching the banister, the speaker says, “understand that leaving is a kind of carrying,” which marks the poem’s insight.

items.prompt: In the third stanza, the pale squares on the wall “look startled to be shown so plain.” What is the effect of this wording?
items.answer: It gives the wall human feelings, making the empty house seem exposed.

wrong.text: It suggests the speaker was frightened by something unseen inside the house.
wrong.why: Confuses the walls’ “startled” look with the speaker’s own fear.

wrong.text: It suggests the walls were damaged during the move.
wrong.why: Reads “startled” as physical harm rather than personification.

wrong.text: It shows the speaker is angry at the people who bought the house.
wrong.why: Nothing in the stanza mentions the buyers.

items.explanation: Calling the squares “startled” is personification that stresses how bare the rooms look.

items.prompt: In the last line, the speaker moves from the physical rooms to “some quiet room of me.” How does this shift develop the poem’s meaning?
items.answer: It moves from outer objects to inner memory, showing the home lives on inside the speaker.

wrong.text: It repeats the first stanza’s picture to show that nothing about the house or the speaker has changed.
wrong.why: The first stanza’s ocean-in-a-shell image is transformed, not repeated.

wrong.text: It shows that the speaker will return to the house soon.
wrong.why: The door “clicks shut” and no return is suggested.

wrong.text: It contrasts a loud house with a quieter new home.
wrong.why: The new home is never described.

items.explanation: The final image turns the house into something internal, supporting the idea that memories continue after leaving.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the passage best supports the claim that the dance tells bees how valuable a food source is?
items.answer: Bees repeat the dance more often and with more energy when food is especially rich.

wrong.text: The straight, shaking stretch is the part that carries the message.
wrong.why: Describes the part of the dance that matters, not food quality.

wrong.text: A quick, short waggle points to a patch just outside the hive.
wrong.why: Shows distance, not value.

wrong.text: Because the sun moves across the sky, the dancers gradually change their angle over the day.
wrong.why: Explains direction, not how rich the food is.

items.explanation: Paragraph 4 links more repetitions and more energy to richer food, so the dance signals quality.

items.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the central idea of the passage?
items.answer: Honeybees use a patterned dance to share the direction, distance, and quality of food.

wrong.text: Honeybees depend on the sun more than other insects do.
wrong.why: Compares bees to other insects, which the passage never does.

wrong.text: Scientists have only recently learned how bees find flowers.
wrong.why: The passage gives no timeline for the discovery.

wrong.text: Honeybees dance mainly to keep the hive warm and to keep the crowded colony together at night.
wrong.why: Invents a purpose; the dance’s purpose is communication.

items.explanation: Each body paragraph explains what the dance communicates: direction, distance, and how worthwhile a food source is.

items.prompt: According to the third paragraph, how are the dance’s angle and the sun connected?
items.answer: The angle from straight up on the comb matches the angle from the sun’s direction to the flowers.

wrong.text: The bees dance in direct sunlight on the hive’s outer wall to show other bees exactly where they should fly next.
wrong.why: The dance happens inside the dark hive.

wrong.text: Gravity pulls the bees toward the sun, so they waggle upward.
wrong.why: Mixes up gravity’s role as a vertical reference with the sun’s direction.

wrong.text: The sun’s brightness tells the bees how far away the flowers are.
wrong.why: Confuses direction, shown by angle, with distance, shown by waggle length.

items.explanation: The paragraph says straight up stands for the sun’s direction, so angles from vertical match angles from the sun.

items.prompt: In the third paragraph, “stand-in” is used in the phrase “straight up as a stand-in for the position of the sun.” What does “stand-in” mean here?
items.answer: a substitute that takes the place of something else

wrong.text: a measuring tool that bees use to track the sun’s movement
wrong.why: Mistakes the phrase for a scientific tool.

wrong.text: a barrier that blocks sunlight from the hive
wrong.why: Takes “stand” literally and thinks of something that blocks.

wrong.text: a signal that warns of danger near the flowers
wrong.why: Associates the dance with warnings rather than directions.

items.explanation: Straight up replaces the sun’s direction inside the hive, so “stand-in” means a substitute.

items.prompt: How does the second paragraph contribute to the development of the passage?
items.answer: It describes the pattern of the dance so that later paragraphs can explain what each part means.

wrong.text: It argues that the waggle dance is the most advanced insect behavior.
wrong.why: Offers an opinion the passage never makes.

wrong.text: It compares the dance to the way humans use language.
wrong.why: The comparison appears only in the final paragraph, and only in a general way.

wrong.text: It lists the discoveries that scientists have made about bees over many years of careful study.
wrong.why: The paragraph describes movement, not discoveries.

items.explanation: Paragraph 2 describes the straight run and loops, and paragraphs 3 and 4 then explain what the angle and length of the run mean.

items.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that measuring depth with a weighted rope was impractical in deep water?
items.answer: The rope could drift or run out of length, and one measurement could take hours.

wrong.text: Sailors tied a lead weight to the end of a long rope.
wrong.why: Describes the method rather than its limits.

wrong.text: The method worked well enough in harbors, according to the crews who used it every day.
wrong.why: True, but it describes where the method worked.

wrong.text: The crew counted how much line ran out before the weight stopped.
wrong.why: Explains how the method was used, not why it failed.

items.explanation: The second paragraph names drifting, running out of rope, and time as the problems in deep water.

items.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
items.answer: Ocean-floor mapping has moved from slow rope soundings to sound-based tools, though much remains unmapped.

wrong.text: Echo sounders have replaced every other way of studying the oceans, and ships now use them to map every part of the seafloor.
wrong.why: Over-generalizes; the passage discusses depth mapping only.

wrong.text: Maps of the seafloor are mainly used to help ships avoid hazards.
wrong.why: Too narrow; the passage names several uses.

wrong.text: Sailors long believed the seafloor was flat until multibeam sonar.
wrong.why: Unsupported claim that is not in the text.

items.explanation: The passage traces rope soundings, echo sounders, and multibeam systems, and ends by noting how much is still unmapped.

items.prompt: How does the echo-sounder method compare with the rope-and-weight method?
items.answer: Both find the distance to the bottom, but the echo sounder uses the time an echo takes to return.

wrong.text: Both depend on the speed of sound in water, but the rope method is less exact.
wrong.why: Gives the rope method a sound-based mechanism it does not have.

wrong.text: The rope method measures depth directly while the echo sounder measures only width.
wrong.why: Mistakes what the echo sounder measures; it also measures depth.

wrong.text: Both require the ship to stop moving during each measurement, but the echo sounder is much cheaper to run.
wrong.why: Cost and stopping are not discussed in the passage.

items.explanation: Paragraphs 2 and 3 show both methods find depth, one using a lowered weight and the other timing an echo.

items.prompt: In the first paragraph, the ocean floor is described as “as hidden as the far side of the moon.” What does this comparison suggest?
items.answer: The seafloor was long unseen and unknown to people.

wrong.text: The seafloor is dangerous to approach.
wrong.why: Confuses hidden with dangerous.

wrong.text: The seafloor looks much like the surface of the moon.
wrong.why: Reads the comparison as similarity of appearance.

wrong.text: The seafloor is uninteresting to scientists.
wrong.why: Reads “hidden” as boring; the passage describes mapping as valuable.

items.explanation: The far side of the moon cannot be seen from Earth, and the next sentence says the seafloor was “largely guesswork.”

items.prompt: In the last paragraph, how does the author respond to the view that satellites have already mapped the seafloor?
items.answer: The author grants that satellites show broad shapes but explains that sonar gives sharper detail.

wrong.text: The author dismisses the view without giving any reason.
wrong.why: Gives a reason; the paragraph explains satellites’ limits.

wrong.text: The author agrees that satellites have replaced ships entirely and that sonar is now outdated for mapping.
wrong.why: Reverses the author’s response.

wrong.text: The author argues that satellites are too expensive to use.
wrong.why: Cost is never mentioned in the paragraph.

items.explanation: The author acknowledges satellites “suggest broad shapes” and then explains that sonar offers “far sharper detail.”

items.prompt: Which detail best supports the claim that green roofs can lower a building’s energy use?
items.answer: The extra layers insulate, so less energy is needed for heating and cooling.

wrong.text: Designers often choose sedum, a hardy plant that tolerates drought, wind, and poor soil.
wrong.why: Describes plant choice, not energy use.

wrong.text: A green roof soaks up much of the rain that falls on it.
wrong.why: Supports the water benefit, not energy savings.

wrong.text: Installation costs more than a conventional roof.
wrong.why: A drawback that does not show lower energy use.

items.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the added layers insulate the building, reducing heating and cooling needs.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
items.answer: Green roofs bring several benefits to buildings and cities, though they have costs and limits.

wrong.text: Green roofs are the best way to prevent flooding in cities.
wrong.why: Over-generalizes one benefit into the main point.

wrong.text: Sedum is the only plant that can survive on a rooftop, so designers use it on every green roof.
wrong.why: Misreads “often choose” as “only.”

wrong.text: Older buildings cannot support green roofs, so they are impractical.
wrong.why: Takes one drawback and treats it as the whole message.

items.explanation: The passage covers benefits in paragraphs 3 and 4 and drawbacks in paragraph 5.

items.prompt: According to the fourth paragraph, how are dark roofs connected to the temperature of city centers?
items.answer: They absorb sunlight and warm the nearby air, helping make city centers hotter.

wrong.text: They trap rainwater that evaporates and heats the air.
wrong.why: Mixes up the rain discussion with the heat discussion.

wrong.text: They reflect sunlight and cool the streets below them.
wrong.why: Reverses what dark surfaces do.

wrong.text: They are heavier than green roofs, so the buildings under them need much more energy for cooling.
wrong.why: Weight is discussed only for wet soil.

items.explanation: The paragraph says dark roofs absorb sunlight and warm the air, “one reason” city centers run hotter.

items.prompt: The last paragraph calls a green roof “part sponge, part blanket, and part garden.” What is the effect of these comparisons?
items.answer: They sum up the roof’s jobs of soaking up water, insulating, and growing plants.

wrong.text: They suggest green roofs are soft and easy to damage.
wrong.why: Reads the images as describing texture only.

wrong.text: They show the author doubts that green roofs will last long enough to repay their cost.
wrong.why: The author is positive about the idea’s spread.

wrong.text: They introduce three new benefits not discussed earlier.
wrong.why: Each image points back to ideas already covered.

items.explanation: The sponge refers to rainwater, the blanket to insulation, and the garden to the plants, bringing earlier ideas together.

items.prompt: How does the fifth paragraph affect the development of the passage?
items.answer: It balances the earlier benefits by presenting drawbacks and a response to them.

wrong.text: It reverses the central claim by arguing that green roofs are impractical for cities.
wrong.why: The passage keeps a positive overall view.

wrong.text: It introduces another benefit related to temperature.
wrong.why: Temperature was covered in the previous paragraph.

wrong.text: It repeats the details about plants from the second paragraph.
wrong.why: The paragraph covers weight and cost.

items.explanation: Paragraph 5 begins with “not without drawbacks” and includes supporters’ replies, giving a fuller picture.

items.prompt: Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that many students need a quiet place to study?
items.answer: In a student council survey, 140 of 200 eighth graders said they struggle to find one.

wrong.text: The library doors close at 3:15 every afternoon.
wrong.why: True, but it states when the library closes, not who needs it.

wrong.text: The library has a beautiful blue carpet that was installed three years ago by the school.
wrong.why: A detail about decoration, not about studying.

wrong.text: The author’s cousin attends a school in another state.
wrong.why: Offers a personal connection, not evidence about students here.

items.explanation: The survey results in paragraph 2 directly show that many eighth graders lack quiet study space.

items.prompt: How does the first paragraph contribute to the development of the argument?
items.answer: It states the author’s claim and previews the reasons developed in the paragraphs that follow.

wrong.text: It presents the strongest counterargument against the plan and then answers it with new evidence.
wrong.why: The counterargument appears in the fourth paragraph.

wrong.text: It summarizes the survey data collected by the student council.
wrong.why: The data appear in the second paragraph.

wrong.text: It tells a story about a student who could not finish homework.
wrong.why: No such story appears in the paragraph.

items.explanation: The paragraph states that the library should stay open and names two reasons, which paragraphs 2 and 3 then support.

items.prompt: How does the author handle the argument that staying open would cost too much?
items.answer: The author admits the concern is reasonable and then offers a plan that limits the cost.

wrong.text: The author ignores the concern and repeats the main claim.
wrong.why: The fourth paragraph addresses the concern directly.

wrong.text: The author agrees that the concern is correct and then drops the proposal from the argument entirely.
wrong.why: The proposal continues in the conclusion.

wrong.text: The author claims the concern was invented by the school board.
wrong.why: Nothing in the text says this.

items.explanation: The author calls the concern “fair” and then points to parent volunteers and teacher assignments.

items.prompt: Which piece of evidence is LEAST relevant to the author’s claim that the library should stay open after school?
items.answer: The library’s blue carpet was installed three years ago, and blue is the author’s favorite color.

wrong.text: A librarian reported that more teenagers borrowed books after another library extended its hours.
wrong.why: Relevant: it connects longer hours to more reading.

wrong.text: A survey found that many students struggle to find a quiet place to study.
wrong.why: Relevant: it shows a need the library could meet.

wrong.text: Parent volunteers have offered to supervise two afternoons a week.
wrong.why: Relevant: it addresses how the plan could be staffed.

items.explanation: The carpet’s color and the author’s taste do not show whether students need the extra hour.

items.prompt: The author uses the example of a cousin’s school to claim, “Clearly, closing a library hurts students’ grades.” Why is this evidence weak?
items.answer: One case does not prove that the closed library caused the grades to fall.

wrong.text: Evidence from another state can never apply to a school here.
wrong.why: Over-generalizes; outside evidence can help if there is enough of it.

wrong.text: The cousin’s grades are unrelated to the school’s library.
wrong.why: Overstates; the flaw is lack of proof of cause, not that no link is possible.

wrong.text: The author does not say how old the cousin is or what grade she is currently in at school.
wrong.why: Age is not the weakness here.

items.explanation: A single story cannot rule out other causes for lower grades, so it is insufficient to support the claim.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The hikers were so parched after the long climb that they drank the entire jug of water in minutes.” What does “parched” most likely mean?
items.answer: very dry and thirsty

wrong.text: tired and sore
wrong.why: Chooses a feeling that follows a climb but ignores the clue about drinking water.

wrong.text: cold and wet
wrong.why: Opposite of what the clue about thirst suggests.

wrong.text: eager and cheerful
wrong.why: Does not explain why they drank so fast.

items.explanation: Drinking the whole jug quickly suggests the hikers were very thirsty.

items.prompt: The word “benevolent” comes from the Latin roots bene- (“good”) and vol- (“wish”). In the sentence “The scientist’s work was benevolent; every study she led aimed to improve the village’s health,” what does “benevolent” mean?
items.answer: wishing to do good for others

wrong.text: wishing to be admired by others
wrong.why: Mixes up the root meaning with fame.

wrong.text: unwilling to share knowledge
wrong.why: Ignores the positive root bene-.

wrong.text: careful about spending money
wrong.why: Associates “benefit” with money rather than kindness.

items.explanation: Bene- means good and vol- means wish, and the sentence says her studies aimed to improve health.

items.prompt: The prefix dis- often means “apart” or “not.” In the sentence “The council voted to disband the committee after it finished its work,” what does “disband” mean?
items.answer: to break apart a group

wrong.text: to praise a group publicly
wrong.why: Ignores the meaning of dis-.

wrong.text: to enlarge a group
wrong.why: Reverses the direction of the prefix.

wrong.text: to rename a group
wrong.why: Fits “council voted” but not the prefix.

items.explanation: Dis- means apart, and the committee finished, so it was ended.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The old bridge could not bear the weight of the heavy trucks.” Which meaning of “bear” is used here?
items.answer: to hold up

wrong.text: to put up with
wrong.why: Chooses the common meaning “tolerate,” which does not fit a bridge.

wrong.text: to give birth to
wrong.why: Picks the animal or family meaning rather than the one fitting the context.

wrong.text: to carry on a journey
wrong.why: Interprets “carry” as moving something rather than supporting it.

items.explanation: A bridge supports weight, so “bear” means to hold up.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “Although the committee seemed ready to quarrel, the mayor’s calm words had a mollifying effect, and the shouting soon died away.” What does “mollifying” most likely mean?
items.answer: soothing

wrong.text: provoking
wrong.why: Reverses the meaning; the shouting stopped, not grew.

wrong.text: confusing
wrong.why: The sentence says the shouting ended, not that people were puzzled.

wrong.text: distracting
wrong.why: Suggests turning attention away rather than calming anger.

items.explanation: The “calm words” and the dying shouting show that the effect was soothing.

items.prompt: The Latin root aud- means “to hear.” In the sentence “The announcement was barely audible over the roar of the crowd,” what does “audible” mean?
items.answer: able to be heard

wrong.text: easy to understand
wrong.why: Confuses hearing with understanding.

wrong.text: pleasant to listen to
wrong.why: Adds a quality of enjoyment that the root does not carry.

wrong.text: worth repeating aloud
wrong.why: Reads aud- as “speak” instead of “hear.”

items.explanation: Aud- means hear, and the crowd noise made the announcement hard to hear.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The ambassador’s reply was deliberately ambiguous; both sides left the room convinced she had agreed with them.” What does “ambiguous” most likely mean?
items.answer: open to more than one meaning

wrong.text: forceful and direct
wrong.why: Reverses the clue that each side heard its own meaning.

wrong.text: dishonest and false
wrong.why: Confuses vagueness with lying.

wrong.text: lengthy and detailed
wrong.why: Does not match the idea of unclear meaning.

items.explanation: Both sides thought she agreed with them, so her reply could be understood in two ways.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The idea was so novel that no one at the meeting had heard anything like it.” What does “novel” mean here?
items.answer: new and original

wrong.text: long and fictional
wrong.why: Uses the noun meaning, a book, instead of the adjective.

wrong.text: familiar and ordinary
wrong.why: Reverses the clue “no one had heard anything like it.”

wrong.text: confusing and unclear
wrong.why: Assumes new ideas must be hard to follow.

items.explanation: The clue “no one had heard anything like it” shows the idea was new.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “Her voice was a warm blanket on a cold night.” What does this metaphor suggest about her voice?
items.answer: It was comforting and soothing.

wrong.text: It was loud and heavy.
wrong.why: Applies the blanket’s weight instead of its comfort.

wrong.text: It was gentle but not sincere.
wrong.why: Adds an idea about honesty that the image does not suggest.

wrong.text: It was quiet and hard to hear.
wrong.why: Mixes up warmth with softness of volume.

items.explanation: A warm blanket on a cold night brings comfort, so her voice does too.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The twins let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.” What does the idiom mean?
items.answer: They revealed a secret.

wrong.text: They ruined the party decorations.
wrong.why: Takes the idiom literally as spoiling something physical.

wrong.text: They adopted a new pet.
wrong.why: Reads the animal literally.

wrong.text: They forgot the date of the party.
wrong.why: Confuses revealing with forgetting.

items.explanation: “Let the cat out of the bag” means to reveal a secret, and the party was a surprise.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The marathon runner finished all twenty-six miles without a scratch, then twisted her ankle stepping off the curb outside the finish line.” Why is this situation ironic?
items.answer: She survived the hardest part safely but was hurt by an ordinary step.

wrong.text: She expected to win but finished in last place.
wrong.why: Invents an expectation that is not in the sentence.

wrong.text: She was injured before the race and ran anyway.
wrong.why: Reverses the order of events.

wrong.text: She was hurt on a curb, and curbs are always dangerous.
wrong.why: States a general claim instead of the contrast in the event.

items.explanation: Irony arises because the outcome is the opposite of what we expect: a small step causes the injury after the long race.

items.prompt: Chapter is to book as scene is to ___. Which word best completes this analogy?
items.answer: play

wrong.text: actor
wrong.why: Pairs a part with a performer, not a part with its whole.

wrong.text: audience
wrong.why: Pairs a part with the people who watch it.

wrong.text: curtain
wrong.why: Pairs a part with an object on the stage, not the whole.

items.explanation: A chapter is a part of a book, and a scene is a part of a play.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The company announced that it was ‘letting go’ of a quarter of its staff.” What effect does the phrase “letting go” have?
items.answer: It softens the harsh idea of firing workers.

wrong.text: It shows that the workers chose to leave on their own.
wrong.why: Reads “let go” as the workers’ choice.

wrong.text: It makes the layoffs sound more severe than they are.
wrong.why: Reverses the effect, which is to make the news gentler.

wrong.text: It shows that the workers were promoted.
wrong.why: Confuses a positive-sounding phrase with a promotion.

items.explanation: A euphemism replaces a blunt phrase such as “firing” with a gentler one.

items.prompt: A shopper who avoids spending money could be described as thrifty, frugal, economical, or stingy. Which word has the most negative connotation?
items.answer: stingy

wrong.text: thrifty
wrong.why: Treats a positive word as a negative one.

wrong.text: frugal
wrong.why: Treats a neutral-to-positive word as negative.

wrong.text: economical
wrong.why: Ignores that this word suggests wise use of money.

items.explanation: “Stingy” suggests selfishness, while the other words suggest wise care with money.

items.prompt: Read the sentence: “The negotiation was a tightrope walk; one careless remark could send the whole deal crashing down.” What does the figurative phrase mean?
items.answer: The talks demanded great care to avoid a ruinous mistake.

wrong.text: The negotiators were skilled circus performers.
wrong.why: Takes the image literally.

wrong.text: The talks were taking place at a great height.
wrong.why: Reads the image as describing a location.

wrong.text: The deal had already failed before the talks began.
wrong.why: Ignores that the sentence says the deal “could” fall.

items.explanation: A tightrope walk requires balance, so the phrase shows that one error could ruin the talks.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: “To ___ the poem, the class examined each stanza and discussed how its parts fit together.”
items.answer: analyze

wrong.text: memorize
wrong.why: Confuses studying parts with learning by heart.

wrong.text: applaud
wrong.why: Mistakes discussing a poem for praising it.

wrong.text: abbreviate
wrong.why: Mixes up examining with shortening.

items.explanation: Examining parts and how they fit together is what it means to analyze.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: “The coach repeated the final instruction twice to ___ how important it was.”
items.answer: emphasize

wrong.text: conceal
wrong.why: Reverses the purpose of repeating something.

wrong.text: excuse
wrong.why: Confuses stressing with forgiving.

wrong.text: estimate
wrong.why: Confuses stressing with guessing a number.

items.explanation: Repeating an instruction stresses its importance, which is what “emphasize” means.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: “Only evidence that is ___ to the claim belongs in an argument; unrelated facts weaken it.”
items.answer: relevant

wrong.text: identical
wrong.why: Mistakes connected for exactly the same.

wrong.text: familiar
wrong.why: Mistakes well known for related.

wrong.text: sufficient
wrong.why: Confuses having enough evidence with having related evidence.

items.explanation: The sentence calls for evidence that is connected to the claim, which is what relevant means.

items.prompt: Which sentence uses the word “contrast” correctly?
items.answer: The author draws a contrast between the quiet village and the busy city.

wrong.text: The two twins looked so contrasting that no one could tell them apart.
wrong.why: Uses “contrasting” as if it meant “alike.”

wrong.text: She contrasted the cake by mixing the sugar and the flour.
wrong.why: Uses the verb as if it meant “make” or “prepare.”

wrong.text: The contrast of the two trains arrived at noon.
wrong.why: Uses the noun as if it were a plural subject.

items.explanation: A contrast points out differences, and a quiet village and a busy city differ.

items.prompt: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: “The second witness’s story helped to ___ the first account, since every detail matched.”
items.answer: corroborate

wrong.text: refute
wrong.why: Reverses the meaning; matching details support rather than disprove.

wrong.text: summarize
wrong.why: Confuses confirming with shortening.

wrong.text: postpone
wrong.why: Confuses confirming with delaying.

items.explanation: Matching details confirm the first account, and corroborate means to confirm.
